newsitem.title: QATAR: Qatar opens an official stock exchange.
newsitem.headline: Qatar opens an official stock exchange.

text.p: Qatar on Monday officially opened a formal stock exchange which it hopes will encourage citizens to plough their money back into the wealthy Gulf Arab oil state rather than invest in the West's developed financial markets.

"We expect the exchange will encourage Qatari citizens to invest in the private and public sector projects and play a major role in supporting industrial activity in the state," said finance ministry undersecretary Youssef Hussein Kamal.

Kamal was speaking after the Doha Securities Market (DSM) -- which occupies two storeys of a downtown building -- was opened by Minister of Finance, Economy and Trade Sheikh Mohammad bin Khalifa al-Thani.

Qatar, like its Gulf Arab neighbours, is trying to diversify its oil-reliant and state-dominated economy and give the private sector a bigger role. It is also trying to lure back Qatari cash invested in capital markets in the West which analysts estimate to run into hundreds of millions of dollars.
"We expect the turnover to jump 15 to 20 percent a year after the opening of the official exchange," Kamal said.
Last year shares worth $89.3 million were traded on the informal market of 18 firms, capitalised at some $1.9 billion.

Trade on the official exchange will start on Tuesday. The market will then be open from Sunday to Thursday from 9 a.m. to 10.30 a.m. (0600-0730 GMT). Initially, the bourse will be partly computerised but by mid-1998 it is expected to be fully automated with the introduction of a system being set up by Andersen Consulting.

The bourse is open only to Qataris. "But by the year-end or early next year, Gulf nationals may be included," said one official. "We are also considering allowing foreigners to trade at the bourse, but it will take some time."
The DSM has appointed Qatar National Bank, Doha Bank and the Commercial Bank of Qatar as brokers. Four more brokers are to be selected from among 20 firms bidding for the job.

Sheikh Mohammad said a World Bank team would visit Qatar in September to advise on privatisation. "A team from World Bank will arrive in Doha to conduct a survey of our privatisation programme and advise us on how to go about it successfully."
The minister said privatisation was one of Doha's priorities to reform its oil and gas-based economy. He hoped the official stock exchange would play an "important role" in that plan.
Currently five firms in which the state has a stake -- Qatar National Bank, Qatar Insurance, Qatar Navigation, Qatar Shipping and Qatar Industrial Manufacturing -- are traded on the bourse.
Officials expect the number to grow as the government offers part of its equity in other companies -- like Qatar Steel and Qatar Industrial Development Bank -- to its citizens.

The Doha Securities Market has 17 companies on its register. Qatar Electricity and Water -- a 60-40 percent private-public venture -- has been excluded because it "did not transact any business during the past six years", an official said.
